introduction-different-operating-systems.core: Neurodiversity (autism, ADHD, dyslexia and others) means brains process information differently, like different operating systems. Many neurodivergent people have exceptional strengths in pattern recognition, focus or creative problem-solving, which standard practices often filter out.

first_principles.problem: Hiring and workplaces tuned for one cognitive style exclude talented engineers and waste their strengths.
truths: Standard processes favour neurotypical social performance.
derivation: **Re-engineer interviews** to assess skills, not social performance.

analogy.title: Different operating systems
analogy.story: Linux isn't a broken Windows; it runs different software brilliantly when you stop expecting Windows behaviour.
analogy.breaks: Every individual differs, so avoid stereotypes and ask the person.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: The process measured social style, not the job.

check.a: The natural variation in how human brains process information, including conditions like autism, ADHD and dyslexia.

the-spiky-profile-understanding-cognitiv.core: Neurotypical people tend to have fairly flat cognitive profiles, while neurodivergent people often have 'spiky' ones: exceptional strengths in some areas (systemising, focus, pattern detection) alongside challenges in others (executive function, social processing).

first_principles.problem: Managers judge a whole person by their weakest dimension and miss exceptional strengths.
derivation: **Map strengths and challenges** with the person.

analogy.title: A mountain range vs. a plateau
analogy.story: The plateau is uniformly average; the range has peaks higher than any plateau, and valleys too.
analogy.breaks: Not every neurodivergent person has 'superpowers'. Avoid romanticising them.

example.title: Role design around a spiky profile
flow: Peak: deep system debugging, pattern spotting

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Exceptional output on the hardest problems.

example.outcome: people placed where their strengths shine.

check.a: A cognitive profile with large variation: exceptional strengths in some areas alongside challenges in others.

re-engineering-the-interview-breaking-th.core: Standard interviews select for social performance: eye contact, small talk, thinking out loud under time pressure, ambiguous questions. Make them fairer by sharing the format in advance, offering written or take-home options, asking clear, specific questions and assessing actual job skills.

first_principles.problem: Live coding with someone watching and vague 'tell me about yourself' questions filter out strong neurodivergent candidates.
truths: Ambiguity and pressure disadvantage some brains.
Accommodations level the field without lowering the bar.
derivation: **Share** the structure and topics in advance.
**Offer choices**: take-home, pair coding, written answers.

analogy.title: Testing swimmers on the track
analogy.story: You'd reject great swimmers if you only timed them running. Test the actual skill.
analogy.breaks: Accommodations must keep the same standard across candidates, with a different format but the same bar.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All candidates know what a good answer looks like.

code.text:
✗ "Tell me about yourself."
✓ "Describe one system you built: what problem it solved, your role, and one technical trade-off you made."

check.q: How can interviews be adapted for neurodivergent candidates without lowering the bar?
check.a: By changing the format (advance info, written or take-home options, clear questions) while assessing the same skills and standards.

the-work-environment-sensory-and-social-.core: Open offices, constant noise, bright lights, unpredictable schedules and implicit social rules can be exhausting or disabling. Offer quiet spaces, headphones, remote options, predictable routines and explicit norms. Most of these help everyone.

first_principles.problem: A capable engineer burns out from sensory overload and unwritten social expectations, not from the work itself.
truths: Unwritten rules are hard for some people.

analogy.title: Curb cuts in pavements
analogy.story: Designed for wheelchairs, they help parents with prams, cyclists and travellers. Universal design helps everyone.
analogy.breaks: Accommodations should be individual, so ask rather than assume.

example.title: Small changes, big effect
flow: Quiet room booked for deep work
example.outcome: environments where everyone can do their best work.

check.q: Why do accommodations for neurodivergent engineers often benefit everyone?
check.a: Practices like quiet spaces, agendas and explicit norms reduce friction for all, which is the curb-cut effect.

management-the-power-of-literal-communic.core: Indirect, implicit communication ('it might be nice if…', vague deadlines, sarcasm) causes misunderstanding. Say clearly what's needed, why, by when, what 'done' means and how you'll give feedback. It's kinder and more effective for everyone.

first_principles.problem: A manager hints that a task is urgent, the engineer takes it literally as optional, and both are frustrated.
truths: Implicit meaning relies on shared social decoding.
derivation: State **what, why, by when and the definition of done**.
Avoid **hints, sarcasm and idioms** for important points.

analogy.title: Writing an API contract
analogy.story: Ambiguous API docs cause integration bugs, and ambiguous instructions cause human bugs.
analogy.breaks: Literal doesn't mean harsh. Be clear and kind.

example.title: Rewriting a request

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No guesswork, and the work happens.

code.text:
✗ "It'd be great if someone looked at the flaky tests sometime."
✓ "Please fix the 3 flaky tests in #412 by Friday. Done = 20 consecutive green runs. It's top priority this week."

example.outcome: instructions that are understood the same way by everyone.

check.q: Why is literal communication valuable for managers?
check.a: It removes ambiguity and the reliance on implicit social cues, preventing misunderstandings for everyone.

psychological-safety-and-disclosure.core: Neurodivergent engineers only disclose if it's safe. Many hide (mask) at great personal cost. Leaders create safety by normalising differences, offering accommodations to everyone without needing a diagnosis, protecting confidentiality and acting supportively on disclosure.

first_principles.problem: Engineers mask their differences to avoid stigma, burn out, and leave without anyone knowing why.
derivation: Offer **'how do you work best?'** questions to everyone.

analogy.title: A user manual for each colleague
analogy.story: Everyone shares 'how I work best'; no one has to justify their settings.
analogy.breaks: Disclosure is always the person's choice. Never pressure it.

example.title: A 'working with me' document
flow: Everyone writes a short 'how I work best' page

check.q: Why offer accommodations without requiring a diagnosis?
check.a: It removes stigma and barriers, letting people get support without disclosing sensitive information.
